Sleep system.why: Model's coldest 10th-percentile night is 12°F at Lizard Head. A 30°F bag leaves you cold on roughly a third of the nights on this route.
Ground conduction, not air temperature, is what actually ends a night. An R-2 summer pad on frozen ground at 10,000 ft defeats any bag you pair it with.
3 oz for real sleep across 23 nights is one of the best trades on the list.

Shelter.why: THE PICK. Slickrock and frozen ground won't hold stakes, and double-wall manages the condensation you get from big diurnal swings. Worth ~14 oz over a tarp.
Lightest real option and fine for the desert half. On the San Juan nights it is a genuine sufferfest, and it pitches badly on slickrock.
Good compromise: near-tarp weight, real snow shedding. Needs anchors you may not find.

Shelter.spec: Polycryo or DCF, cut to size
Shelter.why: Slickrock and cryptobiotic-adjacent grit shred floors.

Worn / riding.why: One pair. Wash and dry them — the desert air does this in an hour.
Sun hoody wins on the Mojave days; UV index is still 3–6 in October.
Dawn starts are near freezing for two-thirds of the trip.
Worn, not carried. Waterproof shoes stay wet once flooded — pick drainage.

Insulation.why: Worn in camp every night from Oct 6 onward. Hooded is not optional at 10,000 ft.
The layer you actually climb in. Down soaks through with sweat; fleece doesn't.
Doubles as sleepwear. Keeping it dry is what makes the 15°F bag hit its rating.
Legs get ignored and then you're awake at 3am.

Insulation.spec: Down booties, or 2 thick wool pairs
Insulation.why: Cold feet are the single most common reason people don't sleep in the cold.
2 oz that buys roughly 5°F of effective bag rating.
Descending from Cedar Breaks or Lizard Head at 25°F is the coldest you will be.

Wind & wet.why: Precip chance peaks at only ~26%, but at 10,000 ft in late October that's snow.
Wind pants cover 90% of the need at half the weight. Full rain pants if you're riding late October.
Cheaper and lighter than solving wet feet any other way.

Water.why: Longest documented dry stretch is ~60 mi. Six litres covers that plus a dry camp with a margin for a stock tank being empty.
SLEEP WITH IT from Oct 6 onward. One freeze cracks the fibres invisibly and it then passes everything.
Weighs nothing and covers a failed or frozen filter.
Desert stock tanks and silty potholes will clog a filter in a day without one.

Cooking.why: THE PICK. Simple, fast, and October nights aren't cold enough to cripple isopropane if you sleep with the canister. Fuel is stocked in Moab, Escalante, Blanding.
Lightest. But alcohol is slow and inefficient in cold and wind, and a hot dinner does real work for morale at 25°F.
Cold burns fuel faster. Buy the big one; small ones are unreliably stocked.
750 ml so you can rehydrate and drink from the same vessel.
Underrated. A hot drink before you leave the bag at 20°F changes the whole morning.

Food carry.why: Sized by the Hanksville → Blanding carry: 110 mi with Hite closed. Most riders are short here, not on water.
Ringtails and mice at established desert camps, not bears, are the problem.

Electronics.why: Daylight drops from 11h50m to 10h50m across the trip, and the hardest days are last.
Highway 95 and Hwy 145 have real traffic and no shoulder.
Cold roughly halves usable battery. 5–6 days between reliable outlets on the Escalante → Blanding stretch.
No cell service for hours at a time on Hwy 95.
Not optional here. Long unpaved stretches, no traffic, no signal, freezing nights.

Repair.why: Goatheads west of St. George, slickrock cuts east of it.

Repair.spec: Frame pump, boot or dollar bill

Repair.why: The one part no shop between Moab and Durango will have for your frame.
Colorado Plateau dust destroys wet lube in a day.
123,000 ft of climbing means 123,000 ft of descending.

Health.why: Snow and slickrock both reflect. UV stays meaningful all month.
23 consecutive days. Do not economise here.
Dry cold hides dehydration as effectively as heat does.
Carry cash — small-town card readers go down and some places are cash-only.
